title: Routing headroom and quantile latency sweeps
content:
Purpose:
Quick exploratory notes on how routing headroom (available spare capacity) maps to quantile latency behavior for long-context workloads across Llama/Mistral/Qwen variants and hybrid MoE models. Trying to produce a reproducible methodology for: (1) identifying fragile operating points where p99 jumps nonlinearly, (2) root-causing whether jumps are routing backpressure vs operator stalls vs memory thrash, and (3) candidate mitigations we can test in the runtime.

Context / Why this matters:
- Customer incidents show small bursts push p99 from ~220ms to >1200ms for long-context QA pipelines.
- Observed that some MoE deployments (hybrid expert topologies) have a small headroom margin before routing stalls cascade.
- Need a repeatable sweep that we can run in CI to detect regressions and quantify safety margin for autoscale policies.

High-level approach:
1) Define a headroom index (HI) = (capacity - sustained_load)/capacity where capacity is measured by max stable throughput at target latency SLO (p95 target).
2) For each model variant (llama-70b, mistral-34b, qwen-7b, and sample MoE-64e topologies) run a controlled arrival-rate sweep from 20% -> 120% of measured capacity in 5% increments.
3) Use fixed long-context prompts (16k and 32k sequences) with realistic request size distribution (70% short completions, 30% long).
4) Collect per-request traces (router events, kernel stalls, mem allocs), KV cache hit/miss, and internal request state transitions.
5) Compute quantile curves (p50, p90, p95, p99, p999) and a new metric: Router Backpressure Index (RBI) — fraction of requests that experienced queueing inside the router > 5ms.

Experiment infra & commands (notes for reproducibility):
- Platform: dedicated-gpu-pool-2 (A100-same-region)
- Runtime build: release/opt-2025-02-07 + router-probe (PR 1782)
- Load driver: rb-synth-driver v0.9. Used constant-Q poisson arrival to mimic bursts.
- Example run: 
  ./rb-synth-driver --model llama-70b-16k --context 16384 --payload-mix mixes/long_qa.json --arrival-load 0.85 --duration 3600s --collect-traces --out ./runs/llama-70b-85p.json
- Kernel logs collected via async-trace-exporter: /var/log/rt/trace-<run-id>.ndjson

Workload specifics:
- long_qa.json: 70% prompts with expected 64 tokens generation, 30% with 2048 tokens.
- batching policy: default dynamic-batcher (max-batch=32, max-latency-ms=15)
- router config: opportune-routing enabled, max-expert-share 0.12, fallback-policy=drop-to-ffn

Preliminary measurements (selected excerpts):
- llama-70b @ 32k context, measured capacity: ~380 tokens/s (sustained before p95 breach).
  * At HI=0.20 (load=0.80*capacity): p50=110ms, p95=270ms, p99=520ms, RBI=0.3
  * At HI=0.05 (load=0.95*capacity): p50=135ms, p95=340ms, p99=2100ms, RBI=0.78 (sharp increase)
  * Observation: p99 jump accompanied by router queue growth traces where per-request router wait > 50ms and then kernel preemption on reorder.

- mistral-34b @ 16k context, measured capacity: ~720 tokens/s
  * At HI=0.15: p50=75ms, p95=190ms, p99=330ms, RBI=0.12
  * At HI=0.00: p50=88ms, p95=210ms, p99=420ms, RBI=0.21 (more graceful)
  * Observation: Mistral is more tolerant due to lower KV cache working set; routing stalls less frequent but when present correlate with memory pressure on attention operators.

- qwen-7b @ 16k context, measured capacity: ~1250 tokens/s
  * At HI near zero the p99 curve increases but not catastrophically; RBI never exceeded 0.18.
  * Qwen variant shows more steady batching behavior and lower kernel variance for short completions.

- MoE-64e hybrid (Qwen backbone + 64 experts), 16k context:
  * Capacity baseline lower due to routing overhead: ~310 tokens/s.
  * Small headroom (HI <=0.07) shows very nonlinear p99: 800ms -> 4.2s within two increments.
  * Traces show: many requests hit expert hot-spots; expert queueing leads to cross-request memory pressure and kernel preemption. Router re-schedules and some requests keep being retried (see trace snippets below).

Representative trace snippet (abridged):
- request_id=abc123 router.enqueue 14.2ms
- request_id=abc123 router.schedule_expert e=23 wait=38.9ms
- kernel.attn.exec stall=12.1ms (mem-swap?)
- request_id=abc123 router.retry 72ms (expert busy)
- request_id=abc123 completed 4.21s

Root-cause hypotheses (ranked):
1) Router queueing amplification: when experts become bottlenecked, router retries/reassignments increase request lifetime, causing more requests in router, positive feedback.
2) Kernel-level thrash from large per-request working sets (long-context) causing GPU memory evictions and runtime stalls.
3) Scheduling artifacts: thread-pool starvation on host side when many small router tasks spawn; manifests as router wait spikes.

Metrics that correlate best with p99 jumps: RBI (router wait fraction), kernel-stall-ms (sum of stall durations during request), and per-expert queue length percentile. KV cache miss rate is only weakly correlated for MoE since routing dominates.

Short-term mitigations to try (quick experiments):
- Admission control: drop to FFN or smaller model when RBI > 0.5 for X seconds (fast fallback).
- Router backoff heuristics: if expert queue > threshold, probabilistically reassign to less-loaded expert or to FFN path.
- Batching tweaks: reduce max-latency-ms from 15->8ms under low headroom profiles to reduce buildup.
- Kernel-level: preallocate bigger per-request workspace to avoid dynamic reallocs (reduces occasional mem-copy stalls).

Longer-term fixes / research directions:
- Headroom-aware autoscaler: integrate RBI into autoscale triggers instead of just average latency or GPU utilization.
- Model-aware routing: use learned routing policies that prefer balanced expert selection considering downstream kernel cost (e.g., avoid hot experts by predicted token lengths).
- Prefetch + speculative mapping: for long-contexts, prefetch KV slices and speculatively assign secondary experts if hot-spot probability > p. Reduces retries at cost of extra memory.

Validation plan (what to test next week):
1) Implement RBI export to metrics pipeline and run week-long synthetic sweeps to identify natural operating headroom at current Dedicated customers. (owner: Carlos)
2) Small PR for admission fallback: runtime config flag fallback.rbi_threshold=0.5 + test harness. (owner: Rina)
3) Stress test with 2x arrival-variance: check whether probabilistic reassign decreases p99 by >30% for MoE-64e. (owner: Aisha)

Open questions / TODOs:
- How does multi-tenant noisy neighbor behavior change the headroom curves? Need cross-tenant runs.
- What is the cost tradeoff for prefetching experts vs memory pressure at 32k contexts? Instrumentation gap: per-expert memory accounting is coarse.
- Verify whether kernel.attn.exec stall=12ms is device-side kernel waiting for mem copy vs host scheduling; need nvprof-style capture for one replicate.

Notes on reproducibility & dataset:
- Saved run configs and trace exports in runs/2025-02-routing-headroom/
- Synthetic prompt seed pool: prompts/longcontext/seed-v3.json (contains 120 prompts).
- If you re-run, pin runtime hash to the commit in PR 1782 + tag runtime-test/2025-02-07.

Appendix: quick checklist for reviewers:
- [ ] Verify the RBI definition and whether 5ms threshold makes sense for our p95 target.
- [ ] Check the admission control PR for safety (no silent data loss).
- [ ] Confirm that the mistral results are reproducible across two different GPU families (A100 vs H100).

Concluding note:
This doc is intentionally exploratory: the simple RBI index is useful to surface fragile headroom regions quickly. My hypothesis: routing amplification is the dominant nonlinear failure mode for MoE under long-context, and mitigating that at the router-level (backoff/prob reassign + admission control) will buy us meaningful p99 stability without immediate model-quantization changes.
